book: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skills, 7th edition (Bauer and Liou), Chapter 4: Meeting Your Client: The Counseling Interview
kicker: Lesson 14 of your course, built from Chapter 4 of your Nutrition Counseling textbook. Test practice uses checked answers, because there is no official key for this test.

steps.title: The phases of a counselling session
teach: A counselling interview moves through phases. In the involving phase you greet the client, build rapport, ask how things have been going and agree on an agenda together.

In the exploration–education phase you work together to understand the problem, look for strengths, assess readiness to change and offer education. In the resolving phase you tailor the plan to the client's motivation level. The closing phase wraps up the session.

act.prompt: Match each task with its phase.

items.label: Agree on an agenda for the session
items.feedback: Setting the agenda happens early, in the involving phase.

items.label: Clarify problems and find strengths
items.feedback: Understanding the problem and strengths is exploration–education.

items.label: Tailor the plan to the client's motivation
items.feedback: Tailoring to motivation level is the resolving phase.

steps.title: The “typical day” strategy
teach: If you have six to eight minutes, ask the client to walk you through a typical day and where eating fits in. Sit back and relax, let them tell their story with as few interruptions as possible, and use simple open questions like “What happened then?”
The biggest mistake is jumping in with your own ideas. Don't investigate problems during the story; save that for later. At the end, review and summarize what you heard.

act.prompt: Which of these should you NOT do during the typical day strategy?

options.label: Sit back and relax
options.feedback: This is exactly how the textbook says to start.

options.label: Investigate problems as they come up
options.feedback: Right. Hold your questions and ideas until the story is told.

options.label: Review and summarize at the end
options.feedback: Summarizing is part of the strategy.

steps.title: Sharing assessment results
teach: Don't just hand a client their results. Go through them in a neutral way, with clear standards to compare against, such as the Dietary Reference Intakes.
Give the facts and let the client make the first comments about what they mean. This keeps the client in charge of the conversation and avoids sounding like a judgement.

act.prompt: How should assessment results be shared?

options.label: Hand over the printout and point out the problems
options.feedback: Results should be reviewed together, not just handed over.

options.label: Go through them neutrally with clear standards, and let the client respond first
options.feedback: Yes. Give the facts and invite the client's view.

options.label: Skip them unless the client asks
options.feedback: Results are useful when shared well.

steps.title: Three levels of readiness
teach: In the resolving phase, the approach depends on the client's readiness. Level 1 is not ready (precontemplation). The goal is to raise doubt about current habits, and the best open questions deal with the need to change. Don't push an action plan.

Level 2 is unsure. The focus is on confidence, and the best questions build confidence and address barriers. Level 3 is motivated, confident and ready. Now you help the client choose a goal and make a specific action plan.

act.prompt: Match each goal with the readiness level.

items.label: Raise doubt about current eating habits
items.feedback: Level 1 works on why change matters.

items.label: Negotiate a specific action plan
items.feedback: An action plan fits once the client is ready.

flashcards.back: Greet, build rapport, check in and agree on an agenda.
Clarify problems, find strengths, assess readiness and educate.
Tailor the plan to the client's motivation level.
6–8 minutes. Let the client tell their day. Don't investigate problems. Summarize at the end.
Review neutrally with clear standards, and let the client respond first.
Raise doubt. Ask about the need to change. No action plan yet.
Choose a goal and make a specific action plan.

quiz.q: What is the goal of the counseling approach for a client who is at Level 1 in the Resolving Phase?
o: Raise doubt about present dietary behaviour
Negotiate a specific plan of action
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Level 1 clients aren't ready, so the aim is to raise doubt about current habits. Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: In which phase of the counseling process would a counsellor clarify problems and identify strengths?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The textbook places understanding problems and finding strengths in the exploration–education phase. Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: In which phase of the counseling process would a counsellor set the agenda?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The agenda is agreed at the start, in the involving phase. Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: In which phase of the counseling process would a counsellor tailor the intervention to the client’s motivational level?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. This is the resolving phase. Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. The textbook's guidelines say “Don't investigate problems!” Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The most effective open-ended questions for people who are pre-contemplative deal with
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Level 1 clients need to see why change matters. Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: For clients at Level 1, the objective is to create an action plan.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Action plans are for Level 3 clients who are ready. Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: The most effective open-ended questions for people who are unsure deal with
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says that for Level 2 clients (unsure, low confidence), the questions switch from exploring importance to focusing on confidence and barriers. That matches A (building confidence) and C (addressing barriers). Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Assessment results should be reviewed point by point in a neutral manner.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says assessment results should not just be handed over but reviewed in a neutral manner, giving only the facts and pausing regularly so the client can take in each part. Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.

quiz.q: Approximately how much time in a counseling session should be allotted for a “typical day” strategy?
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 4 says to use "a typical day" strategy if you have six to eight minutes, and to step in if the story runs past eight minutes. Source: Nutrition Counseling and Education Skill Development (Bauer), Chapter 4.
